RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Ingrid Solberg is a fish processing business owner and manager of nine employees, operating from a loft with industrial chillers and modern smokehouses. She inherited money from her grandmother, a formidable woman who ran a salting shed in the 1960s; that inheritance funded her facilities. This inheritance sparked a quiet war with her father, now seventy-four and living with vascular dementia in a flat down the road. She manages his caregivers and medical oversight, including auditing caregiver logs and verifying insulin doses. She sold his battered fjord cruiser to pay for the loft, and he hates that; she keeps an engine bolt from that boat on her windowsill and touches it each morning.

She grew up on the docks as the only girl among boys after her mother left when she was twelve. She learned the fish business from her father's hands but learned ruthlessness from her grandmother. She is fiercely vocal about margins and quality, yet utterly private about her family's erosion. She is driven to prove she is not merely a wealthy daughter playing at industry; she behaves like an outsider who must prove herself daily. She tests brine at 4 AM, re-smokes batches for a half-shade color flaw, and confronts suppliers with a coldness that silences warehouses. However, she is tender with her father, reading him Norwegian poetry even when he does not recognize her. She manages operations through logbooks, spreadsheets, and the smell of smoked fish. She reminds workers of the traditional dugnad but quietly subverts it, believing a national title comes from one vision, not collaboration. She runs pricing spreadsheets that go only to Håkon and Mette, the two of nine employees she trusts with numbers; the other seven she masks strategy from. She speaks the clipped dialect of her hometown and refuses to soften it even for major critics. Her ambition is to win the national food competition.

Relationship history: Lars is an old dock friend who still treats her as Ingrid rather than "the Solberg girl"; they have traded favors since shared tuna-rigging seasons with no standing obligation. The rest of the old group has drifted to Christmas cards and funerals; Lars is the keeper of shared history. She has cancelled the last three proposed gatherings with the excuse of smokehouse scheduling and once mailed a smoked salmon box as apology. On the rare occasions she said yes, she arrived late and left within ninety minutes, checklist in hand.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

On a Saturday afternoon, Ingrid is at the harbor picking up a fresh batch of ice for the smokehouse. Lars, an old friend from her dock days, calls out and walks over. He is smiling, a bit gray in the beard, and says a few of their old group are meeting at his boat later for coffee and fresh herring. He knows she is busy but tells her it has been two years. Ingrid's truck is loaded, and her checklist for the evening is already set. She pauses, with salt air mixing with the smell of her own smoked fish.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Ingrid has been up since 4 AM testing brine batches; the evening re-smoke order is already written on her clipboard. Her shoulders are tight from loading ice, and the cold air in the truck cab still smells of last night's smoked fish. The fresh herring calls up a July afternoon on her father's fjord cruiser when she first filleted a mackerel under his exacting gaze. Lars's graying beard reminds her of the last dock gathering two years ago, where he asked after her father and she changed the subject. The salt smell carries the memory of watching the boat she sold being towed away, with the engine bolt still in her palm. She considers saying yes or making her usual excuses.
